title: Only what he strives for
hookLine: a person has only what he strives for, and his striving will be seen (53:39–40)

cards: Day six hundred. However those mornings came, with full attention, half-asleep, or pressing play just to keep the streak alive, they were somebody's effort. A milestone invites a tally: days, streaks, minutes.
Surah An-Najm keeps a different kind. It's about what a person ends up holding at the end: not what they hoped for, not what they inherited, not what someone said about them.
What they actually strove for, and nothing else.

teach.b: Verses thirty-nine and forty, in Pickthall's translation: "And that man hath only that for which he maketh effort, And that his effort will be seen." The word is sa'y: striving, effort, going toward something on purpose.
If you've followed the pilgrimage, you've met it.

The sa'y is the walk, seven times, between the hills of Safa and Marwah, remembering Hajar running between them searching for water for her baby, Isma'il. Effort as a body moving toward what it needs.
The verse sits in a passage the surah says was in the scrolls of Musa and of Ibrahim: no soul carries another's burden, and a person has only what they strive for. Two promises come out of it.
Nobody can take your effort from you, or be credited with it in your place.

teach.h: YOURS, AND IT WILL BE SEEN.
teach.b: And it will be seen, not necessarily by people. Seen. Scholars raise an honest question here.

teach.h: WHAT REACHES THE DEAD? SCHOLARS WEIGH IT.
teach.b: What about charity given for the dead, or prayers for a parent who's gone? Hadith in Bukhari and Muslim say such things do reach the dead. Scholars reconcile it in different ways.
Some say a righteous child is part of the parent's own striving: a hadith in Muslim names a good child who prays for you among the three things that continue after death.
Others say the verse sets the rule of justice, and Allah's generosity can add to it. Either way, in the verse's words, a person's effort is theirs, and it will be seen.

how: Pilgrims perform the sa'y, walking seven times between Safa and Marwah in memory of Hajar; Muslims also give charity and pray on behalf of parents who have died, as hadith describe.

o: a reward handed down from one's parents
the circling of the Ka'bah during Hajj
effort, striving toward something on purpose

games.q: only what he strives for — tap the pairs.
p: one of three things that continue

s: the sa'y of the pilgrimage shares a word with 53:39
sa'y: effort, the walk between Safa and Marwah.
scholars say nothing anyone does can benefit the dead
hadith say charity and prayer for the dead reach them; scholars reconcile this with the verse.
the surah says this principle was in the scrolls of Musa and Ibrahim

games.q: you give charity for your mother who has died. a friend quotes 53:39. what do the hadith and scholars say?
o: hadith say it reaches her; scholars explain how it fits the verse.
games.why: Bukhari and Muslim report charity for a dead parent reaching them; scholars reconcile it in different ways.

practice: Picture Hajar's walk: back and forth between two hills, looking, not giving up.

Then bring to mind one thing that deserves your real effort, a hard conversation, a task you keep postponing, a person who needs you, and see yourself doing it fully, not halfway. If you pray, ask for strength in it.

wordCard.voice: Sa'y: in 53:39, a person has only their effort, and in 53:40, that effort will be seen. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: striving, effort; also the pilgrimage walk between Safa and Marwah.

carryVoice: Your line: only what you strive for. In the verse's words, it will be seen. Six hundred days, and counting.
